Newborn Tasmanian pademelons weigh a remarkably modest 0.42 grams [Wwb = 0.42 grams], placing them among the smallest neonates relative to adult body size within the Macropodidae. This minuscule birth mass reflects the marsupial reproductive strategy, wherein a highly altricial newborn must complete its development within the maternal pouch following a brief gestation. Under the stable thermal conditions maintained within the pouch, around 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], the gestation period itself is completed in approximately 29 days [tg = approximately 29 days], an exceptionally short duration for a mammal of this ultimate size. Following parturition, the tiny neonate embarks on an arduous climb to the pouch, where it permanently attaches to a teat and begins an extended period of postnatal growth and organogenesis. The extreme altriciality of the pademelon at birth, with a mass several thousand times smaller than that of the adult female, imposes profound constraints on early survival; only a fraction of newborns successfully reach the pouch and establish a secure teat attachment. This developmental pattern stands in contrast to that of eutherian herbivores of comparable adult mass, which typically produce much larger, more developed offspring after a prolonged gestation.

Under the regulated microclimate of the pouch, maintained at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], the developing pademelon young eventually attains a wet weight of 1029 grams [Wwx = 1029 grams] at the point of weaning, marking a substantial increase from the neonatal mass. Weaning represents a critical nutritional transition, as the juvenile shifts from a complete dependence on milk to an exclusive diet of herbaceous forage, and it typically occurs at approximately 202 days since birth [tx = approximately 202 days since birth] at a temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. The timing of this transition is closely tied to the seasonal availability of high-quality pasture, as the young animal must acquire sufficient energy to sustain both growth and thermoregulation outside the pouch. The weaning mass of roughly one kilogram is a substantial fraction of the mother's own body weight, reflecting the high maternal investment in a single offspring each year. This pattern of producing a single, well-developed juvenile annually is characteristic of many medium-sized macropodids inhabiting temperate environments where seasonal resource pulses dictate the optimal window for reproductive effort.

As the weaned juvenile continues to grow, it must acquire sufficient body reserves to support the onset of reproductive maturation. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic regime, at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 435 days since birth [tp = approximately 435 days since birth], indicating that sexual maturity is not attained until well into the second year of life. This protracted period of juvenile development is associated with the need to reach a adequate body mass before reproduction becomes feasible. Indeed, the maximum body mass attained by healthy adults in the wild, often termed the ultimate wet weight, reaches approximately 5000 grams [Wwi = approximately 5000 grams], a threshold that reflects the species' allocation of resources to somatic growth before diverting energy toward reproductive functions. Females will typically defer their first breeding attempt until they have accumulated substantial fat reserves, ensuring that they can meet the high energetic demands of gestation and lactation. This conservative life-history strategy, with delayed maturity and moderate adult size, is consistent with that of other browsing macropodids inhabiting predictable, temperate environments where competition for quality forage can be intense.

The reproductive output of the Tasmanian pademelon is characterized by an exceptionally slow pace, with females producing a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] under the stable thermal conditions (35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]) that support optimal metabolic function. Each litter consists of a single offspring [N_R_i = Each litter consists of a single offspring], a pattern typical of many medium-sized macropodids and one that maximizes per-offspring investment in a competitive environment. This slow reproductive schedule is likely an adaptation to the seasonal unpredictability of Tasmania's temperate forests, where the availability of high-quality forage for both the mother and the developing young is highly variable. It also reflects the high energetic cost of producing a single, large, well-developed offspring that can survive its first winter independently. Consequently, population growth rates are inherently slow, making the species vulnerable to sustained increases in adult mortality from any source.

Long-term field records indicate that the maximum lifespan of the Tasmanian pademelon in the wild is approximately 8.8 years [am = approximately 8.8 years], with the longest-lived individuals documented under the ambient thermal conditions characteristic of their temperate habitat (35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]). This lifespan is relatively extended for a mammal of its body size, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and iteroparity over high annual fecundity. The extended period of reproductive activity afforded by a long lifespan allows females to produce several litters over their lifetime, partially compensating for the low annual reproductive output. Senescence in this species is marked by a gradual decline in body condition, tooth wear, and a reduced ability to compete for high-quality foraging patches, which ultimately leads to an increased vulnerability to starvation during harsh winters. The combination of these traits defines a conservative, slow-paced life history well-suited to the relatively stable but resource-limited forest ecosystems of Tasmania, and such life-history patterns render the species less resilient to rapid environmental perturbations or novel stressors like habitat fragmentation.
